analysis.one_liner: Blocks the government from finalizing new limits on how many hours truck drivers can work.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote: it was introduced with zero cosponsors and died in the Senate Commerce Committee when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In May 2000, the government's truck-safety agency proposed new rules limiting how many hours commercial truck drivers can work before resting. Senator Ben Nighthorse Campbell introduced this bill to forbid the Transportation Department and its safety agency from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing that rule. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, trucking companies would have been spared the cost of the proposed hours-of-service limits, which would have restricted driver schedules and required more rest time. Shippers and carriers whose business models depend on long or flexible driver hours would have avoided the compliance costs of the rule.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have barred the Secretary of Transportation and the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration from taking any action to finalize, implement, or enforce the proposed 'Hours of Service of Drivers' rule published May 2, 2000.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, truck drivers would have continued working under older, less restrictive hours rules, and the public would bear the safety risk of fatigued commercial drivers on the road. The proposed rule was written to address driver fatigue, a known factor in truck crashes.

drawbacks.text: The proposed hours-of-service rule would have imposed real compliance costs on motor carriers, including scheduling constraints that carriers argued could reduce flexibility and income for some drivers who are paid by the mile or load rather than by the hour.
A one-senator bill with no cosponsors cannot realistically become law, so the effort amounted to a symbolic objection to the rule rather than a credible path to stopping it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For trucking companies, the bill's value was avoiding the cost of new scheduling limits. For drivers and the traveling public, blocking the rule would have left in place older hours standards that the safety agency had concluded needed updating to address fatigue. The bill never advanced far enough for this tradeoff to be decided.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Commerce Committee in June 2000 and stayed there; with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors, it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Ben Nighthorse Campbell introduced the bill in the Senate on June 13, 2000 and gave introductory remarks the same day.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action was taken on the bill; it never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the Senate or House.

The bill would have prohibited the Transportation Department and the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing the proposed Hours of Service of Drivers rule.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the proposed safety rule was not blocked by statute, and trucking companies did not get the legislative shield they sought. Truck drivers and the public were spared a law that would have prevented the hours-of-service update.

for.name: Sen. Ben Nighthorse Campbell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its introductory remarks on June 13, 2000.

for.name: American Trucking Associations
for.role: National trade association for motor carriers
for.what_they_did: The trucking industry publicly opposed the proposed hours-of-service rule, and this bill aligned with that industry position, though the record does not show the association backing this specific bill.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill; it received no markup or vote and died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan lineup was recorded.

industries.note: Passage would have spared carriers the cost and scheduling constraints of the proposed hours-of-service rule. The industry's gain would have come at the expense of driver rest rules aimed at reducing fatigue-related crashes.

The proposed rule would have limited how long drivers can be required to work, addressing fatigue. Some drivers paid by the mile could face scheduling changes, but the rule's core purpose was protecting their rest and safety.
